body:
If your dog has just been diagnosed with lymphoma, or you are the veterinarian helping an owner weigh options, this page lists the canine lymphoma clinical trials labeled recruiting in the VetTrials trial database snapshot checked November 3, 2026. There are ten: treatment studies (including two CAR-T cell studies, a BTK inhibitor and a virus-based therapy), studies that collect samples while dogs receive standard chemotherapy, and two screening studies, one of which is only for healthy dogs.

Read the entries, note the ones that match your dog's lymphoma type and treatment history, and take them to your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist. Timing matters: several studies only accept dogs that have not started chemotherapy or steroids yet. You can also run the [live lymphoma trial search](https://vettrials.org/?q=lymphoma&species=dog&status=recruiting) for the newest listings.

## Why B-cell or T-cell matters for which canine lymphoma clinical trials fit

Lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes, a type of immune cell, and of lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow. Penn Vet's oncology service calls it one of the most common cancers diagnosed in dogs, and notes that the multicentric form, which involves the external lymph nodes, is the most common ([Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)). Often the only sign an owner notices is swollen lymph nodes under the neck, in front of the shoulders or behind the knees ([Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)).

Canine lymphoma is grouped by the type of lymphocyte it comes from: B-cell or T-cell ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs)). A test on the tumor sample, often flow cytometry or a PCR test called PARR, sorts out which one your dog has ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs); [Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)). This label, called the immunophenotype, matters for trials. Most of the treatment studies below are written for B-cell lymphoma, and some go further and require large-cell or high-grade disease. One study is specifically for T-cell lymphoma, and the virus-based study accepts aggressive lymphoma of either type. Published sources describe the outlook as generally different between the two types ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs)), and one of the listed studies exists because T-cell outcomes vary more than once thought ([Ontario Veterinary College](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/evaluating-the-clinical-outcome-of-dogs-diagnosed-with-t-cell-lymphoma/)).

Trials also use staging. The World Health Organization system runs from stage I (a single lymph node or one organ's lymphoid tissue) to stage V (blood, bone marrow or other organ involvement), with a substage "b" for dogs that are sick from the disease, for example with fever or weight loss ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs)). Some studies below set limits on stage, substage or the number of enlarged nodes.

## How canine lymphoma is usually treated

Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment because lymphoma is a whole-body disease ([Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)). The most common combination is a CHOP-based protocol: cyclophosphamide, hydroxydaunorubicin (doxorubicin), vincristine and prednisone, sometimes with L-asparaginase added ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs)). Penn Vet describes these drugs being given on a weekly basis for several months, and notes that single-agent protocols can be used when medical, practical or financial limits apply ([Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)).

Penn Vet is also clear about what treatment usually achieves: most dogs on a CHOP protocol go into remission, a remission is the temporary disappearance of detectable cancer rather than a cure, and most dogs relapse at some point ([Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/lymphoma-in-dogs.pdf)). For cost questions about standard chemotherapy, see our guide to what dog chemotherapy costs.

## Timing: prior treatment can affect eligibility

The detail that most often decides eligibility is what treatment a dog has already had. Among the studies on this page, the Georgia study excludes dogs that have had prior lymphoma treatment or more than 14 days of prednisone ([University of Georgia](https://vet.uga.edu/clinical-trial/dogs-diagnosed-with-b-cell-lymphoma/)). The Iowa State screening study excludes dogs with prior prednisone, chemotherapy or immunotherapy ([Iowa State University](https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vmc/clinical-trials/cerumen-as-a-biomatrix-for-canine-lymphoma-screening/)). The Guelph T-cell study requires no previous steroids or chemotherapy ([Ontario Veterinary College](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/evaluating-the-clinical-outcome-of-dogs-diagnosed-with-t-cell-lymphoma/)). Cornell's study allows prior prednisolone only ([Cornell University](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/smart-start-therapy-canine-b-cell-lymphoma)). The Minnesota CAR-T study restricts prednisone and several immune-modifying drugs ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/car-t-cell)).

Prednisone on its own can improve quality of life for a time ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/circulatory-system/lymphoma-in-dogs/lymphoma-in-dogs)), so the question of whether to start it can come up within days of a diagnosis. If a trial is something you want to consider, raise it with your veterinarian before any treatment begins, so the decision about steroids is made with the trial rules in view. This is a conversation for your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist; only they can weigh it against your dog's condition.

## Lymphoma trials listed as recruiting (checked November 3, 2026)

Each study below is listed as recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. That database label is not confirmation that the institution is currently enrolling. Status and details can change at any time, so confirm with the institution before planning around one. VetTrials is an independent listing site, not the enrolling institution, and is not affiliated with AVMA's Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry or with any of the universities listed. See [About VetTrials](https://vettrials.org/about) for how listings work.

### Treatment studies for B-cell lymphoma

### [LEAH xCAR-T: Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/65)

University of Missouri, Columbia, MO. A CAR-T cell study for dogs with large cell B-cell lymphoma. This study uses xenogeneic CAR-T cells, rather than cells made from the patient’s own blood, along with lymphodepleting chemotherapy ([University of Missouri](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)). The listing describes dogs over 10 kg with newly diagnosed or relapsed disease that are clinically well, meet bloodwork requirements, have no primary gastrointestinal or lung involvement, and are not receiving immunomodulatory drugs. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)

### [CAR-T cell therapy for canines with B-cell lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/676)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. A pilot study, sponsored by LEAH Labs according to the institution's page, checking the safety of a CAR-T cell therapy in dogs with CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma. The institution's page lists dogs of at least 10 kg (any breed except boxers) with multicentric lymphoma, at least four measurable peripheral lymph nodes, new or relapsed disease, and substage a only ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/car-t-cell)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page describes the study as fully funded for the outlined visits. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/car-t-cell)

### [Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/329)

University of Missouri, Columbia, MO. Tests BI705564, an investigational drug that blocks Bruton's tyrosine kinase, a key signaling molecule in the B-cell receptor pathway that helps drive growth and survival of B-cell lymphoma cells ([Harrington et al., PLoS One](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4951150/)). The listing describes dogs older than 1 year, 10 to 50 kg, with newly diagnosed, untreated B-cell lymphoma confirmed with immunophenotyping, at least two peripheral lymph nodes of 2 cm or more, and WHO stage II to IV disease. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)

### [Dogs diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/204)

University of Georgia, Athens, GA. An exploratory field study of an investigational veterinary product (not named on the listing) for large B-cell lymphoma. The institution's page lists newly diagnosed, untreated dogs that are 10 to 50 kg and over 12 months old, and excludes prior lymphoma treatment and more than 14 days of prednisone ([University of Georgia](https://vet.uga.edu/clinical-trial/dogs-diagnosed-with-b-cell-lymphoma/)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page says screening, follow-up visits and the product are provided as part of the study. [Institution page](https://vet.uga.edu/clinical-trial/dogs-diagnosed-with-b-cell-lymphoma/)

### [Smart-Start Therapy for Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/654)

Cornell University, Ithaca, NY. Dogs receive a short pre-treatment drug matched to their tumor's biology, then standard CHOP chemotherapy; there is no placebo. The institution's page lists dogs seen at the Cornell University Hospital for Animals with B-cell lymphoma, no prior treatment other than prednisolone, and owners willing to pursue standard chemotherapy ([Cornell University](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/smart-start-therapy-canine-b-cell-lymphoma)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page describes a contribution toward chemotherapy costs; it did not state an enrollment status when we checked. [Institution page](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/smart-start-therapy-canine-b-cell-lymphoma)

### Treatment study for aggressive B-cell or T-cell lymphoma

### [ORBIT - VSV and an anti-PD-1 inhibitor for Canine Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/190)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. A phase 2 study combining a genetically modified vesicular stomatitis virus with an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/orbit-vsv)). Oncolytic viruses are viruses that replicate preferentially in tumor cells ([Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8662562/)), and checkpoint inhibitors block an "off" signal so T cells can attack cancer cells ([National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/types/immunotherapy/checkpoint-inhibitors)). The institution's page lists dogs with aggressive B-cell or T-cell lymphoma that are untreated or stopped chemotherapy because of resistance, relapse or severe side effects, weigh at least 7.5 kg, are spayed or neutered, and can be kept away from livestock and horses for several days after treatment ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/orbit-vsv)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page says owners pay for initial screening tests and study visits and treatments are covered after enrollment, subject to the study’s stated funding cap. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/orbit-vsv)

### Studies that collect samples or data during standard treatment

These studies do not test a new treatment. Dogs receive standard care, and the study collects samples or information to learn more about the disease.

### [Pilot Study Evaluating the Microbiota in Dogs with Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/274)

Oregon State University, Corvallis, OR. Studies the bacteria living in and on dogs (nasal, oral and rectal swabs) before and during chemotherapy, and whether changes relate to side effects or response. Dogs receive either a CHOP protocol or single-agent doxorubicin ([Oregon State University](https://vetmed.oregonstate.edu/oncology-clinical-trials)). The listing describes dogs with newly diagnosed multicentric lymphoma, at least 1 year old and 15 kg, otherwise healthy. Cost coverage noted in the listing: partial. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.oregonstate.edu/oncology-clinical-trials)

### [Evaluating the Clinical Outcome of Dogs Diagnosed with T-cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/303)

Ontario Veterinary College, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON (Canada). A study aimed at more accurate prognosis for T-cell lymphoma. If T-cell lymphoma is confirmed, an extra needle-core lymph node biopsy is taken under sedation ([Ontario Veterinary College](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/evaluating-the-clinical-outcome-of-dogs-diagnosed-with-t-cell-lymphoma/)). The institution requires confirmed T-cell lymphoma with no previous steroids or chemotherapy. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page says the study covers the biopsy costs; it did not state an enrollment status when we checked. [Institution page](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/evaluating-the-clinical-outcome-of-dogs-diagnosed-with-t-cell-lymphoma/)

### Screening studies, including one for healthy dogs

### [LYRA 3 - blood collection study for lymphoma in healthy dogs at least 5 years old](https://vettrials.org/trial/187)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. This study is for healthy dogs, not dogs with lymphoma. It collects blood to help build a test that could flag dogs at high risk of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; no treatment is offered. The institution's page lists dogs at least 5 years old with no history of cancer, living in the contiguous United States, with samples drawn at your own veterinarian's clinic and health surveys every 6 months ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/lyra-3-blood)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. The institution's page says the kit and shipping are covered and office visit costs are the owner's. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/lyra-3-blood)

### [Cerumen as a Biomatrix for Canine Lymphoma Screening](https://vettrials.org/trial/266)

Iowa State University, Ames, IA. A screening research study comparing earwax (cerumen) from healthy dogs and dogs with multicentric lymphoma, collected with ear swabs. It enrolls both healthy dogs and untreated dogs with lymphoma; no treatment is offered ([Iowa State University](https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vmc/clinical-trials/cerumen-as-a-biomatrix-for-canine-lymphoma-screening/)). Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.iastate.edu/vmc/clinical-trials/cerumen-as-a-biomatrix-for-canine-lymphoma-screening/)

## What "recruiting" means on this page

"Recruiting" on this page means recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. It does not establish the institution's current enrollment status. It is not a promise that a spot is open today or that your dog qualifies. Studies fill, pause and close, and some institution pages do not show a status at all. The study team decides eligibility after its own screening, which may include tests at your expense. Treat every entry as a reason to ask, then confirm directly with the institution and with your veterinarian.

## What joining a trial can involve

Trials sponsored through the National Cancer Institute's comparative oncology program are reviewed for animal welfare and scientific merit, often offer substantial financial support, and do not prevent a dog from receiving conventional treatment after the study ends ([National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)). Individual studies differ widely, though. The Minnesota CAR-T study, for example, involves a screening visit, several days of pre-treatment, an overnight stay and follow-up visits over about three months ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/car-t-cell)). Others need little more than a blood draw or an ear swab. Travel, visit frequency and which costs fall to you vary by study, so ask early. Our broader guide to dog cancer clinical trials covers the general process.

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how soon would my dog need to start?
- Does my dog's lymphoma type, stage and treatment history (including any prednisone) fit?
- What does screening involve, and who pays for it if my dog does not qualify?
- How many visits are needed, how long do they last, and are overnight stays expected?
- Which costs are covered, which are mine, and what happens if side effects need care?
- Can my dog receive standard chemotherapy during or after the study?
- Can my regular veterinarian handle any visits or samples?
- Who do I call with questions after hours?

title: Clinical Trials for Dogs With Bladder Cancer (TCC)
heading: Bladder Cancer in Dogs (TCC): Clinical Trials
description: Bladder cancer (TCC) trials for dogs listed as recruiting on Nov 3, 2026, with notes on each study, what TCC is, typical treatment and what to ask.

cta.heading: Search bladder cancer trials for dogs
cta.text: The live search for "bladder" also returns gallbladder studies. Look for listings that mention bladder tumors, transitional cell carcinoma or urothelial carcinoma.

body:
If your dog has been diagnosed with bladder cancer, most often transitional cell carcinoma (TCC), this page lists the clinical trials for dogs with bladder cancer labeled recruiting in the VetTrials trial database snapshot checked November 3, 2026: three bladder tumor studies at two veterinary schools, plus one related prostate cancer study. Each entry links to the listing and to the institution's own page.

Read the note under each study before you call (one university page shows an enrollment end date that has already passed). Then take the list to your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist, who can judge which studies fit your dog's diagnosis, tumor location and overall health. You can also run the [live bladder search](https://vettrials.org/?q=bladder&species=dog&status=recruiting) yourself; it also returns gallbladder studies, which are a different organ and condition.

## What TCC and urothelial carcinoma mean

Transitional cell carcinoma and urothelial carcinoma are two names for the same cancer. It starts in the transitional cells that line the urinary tract, which runs from the kidneys through the ureters and bladder to the urethra ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)). Trial listings and newer papers often use "urothelial carcinoma" or "invasive urothelial carcinoma" (InvUC), so it helps to search for both terms.

Purdue University's bladder cancer research program describes the most common bladder cancer in dogs as invasive TCC of intermediate to high grade, and notes that bladder cancer makes up about 2% of all cancers in dogs ([Purdue Veterinary Medicine](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). Some breeds carry much higher risk. Purdue reports that Scottish Terriers have an 18 to 20 fold higher risk than other dogs, and that Shetland Sheepdogs, Beagles, West Highland White Terriers and Wire Hair Fox Terriers are 3 to 5 times more likely to develop TCC ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)).

Where the tumor sits matters a great deal. These tumors are frequently found at the trigone (the neck of the bladder, where the ureters enter) or in the urethra, which makes complete surgical removal unlikely in most cases ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)). TCC can also involve the kidneys, ureters, prostate and urethra ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). Many trial criteria depend on tumor location, size and spread, so ask your veterinarian for the imaging and pathology reports before you contact a study team.

The most common signs are blood in the urine, straining to urinate and frequent attempts to urinate. Purdue points out that urinary tract infections can cause the same signs, which is one reason a firm diagnosis matters ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)).

## How bladder cancer in dogs is diagnosed and usually treated

A tissue biopsy, taken by surgery, cystoscopy (a camera passed into the bladder) or sometimes a urinary catheter, gives a definitive diagnosis ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). The Merck Veterinary Manual also describes a urine BRAF mutation test as a sensitive and specific noninvasive test, and states that a positive result is diagnostic for TCC/urothelial carcinoma ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)). Studies differ on what they accept: NC State's study page accepts cytology plus a BRAF test, or a biopsy ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)), while Purdue's recruiting study asks for a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis or a strongly suspected mass to be confirmed during the study ([Purdue trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)).

Medical management is the foundation of treatment in most cases, typically a combination of chemotherapy and COX inhibitors (a class of anti-inflammatory drugs), and radiation can be used in some cases ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)). Purdue lists drug options such as piroxicam alone or combined with vinblastine or mitoxantrone, and low-dose metronomic chlorambucil, and notes that stents or cystotomy tubes can relieve a blocked urinary tract ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). Merck states plainly that treatment is not usually curative ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)). Which approach fits a particular dog is a decision for you and your veterinary oncologist.

## Why bladder cancer trials exist

Purdue's trials page notes that although most dogs with TCC respond to treatment at first, the cancer often becomes resistant over time and can come back ([Purdue trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)). New drugs, new combinations, immune-based treatments and better surgical tools are what trials test.

There is also a wider reason. Purdue describes canine TCC as almost identical to human invasive urothelial carcinoma under the microscope, and says studies in pet dogs have already led to clinical trials in people with bladder cancer ([Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). A trial is research: it may or may not help the dog enrolled, and no study on this page promises a result.

## Bladder cancer trials listed as recruiting (checked November 3, 2026)

Each study below is listed as recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. That database label is not confirmation that the institution is currently enrolling. Status, eligibility and costs can change at any time, so confirm everything with the institution. VetTrials is an independent listing site. It is not the enrolling institution and is not affiliated with the AVMA's veterinary clinical trials registry or with any of the universities named here ([about VetTrials](https://vettrials.org/about)).

### [Enrolling Dogs with Invasive Bladder Cancer](https://vettrials.org/trial/106)

NC State University College of Veterinary Medicine, Raleigh, North Carolina. The listing describes an experimental immunotherapy being studied for safety and immune-stimulating effects in dogs with invasive bladder cancer, in an 8-day study. NC State's own page adds that the treatment is given into the bladder under anesthesia, that every dog receives it (no placebo group), and that dogs must weigh at least 8 kg (17.6 lbs) and have a muscle-invasive bladder mass on ultrasound. **Check first:** NC State's page lists an enrollment finish date of September 30, 2026, which has passed, so ask whether the study is still accepting dogs. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. NC State's page says pre-study testing and the immunotherapy, hospitalization and anesthesia are provided at no cost. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)

### [Combination of Lapatinib and Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Transitional Cell Carcinoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/432)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. The study combines a drug called lapatinib with fractionated radiation therapy (radiation given as a series of separate treatments) for dogs with transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. The listing's eligibility note is broad: dogs with TCC who are candidates for this combination. CSU’s current page requires biopsy-confirmed bladder TCC, ability to receive an NSAID and repeated anesthesia, no radiation in the last 6 weeks and no chemotherapy in the last 2 weeks. The database says full coverage, but CSU lists owner-paid initial diagnosis and NSAIDs, with a contribution toward radiation rather than all radiation costs. The study covers lapatinib and specified rechecks and tests. Confirm your remaining bill with the team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/combination-of-lapatinib-and-fractionated-radiation-therapy-for-dogs-with-transitional-cell-carcinoma/)

### [Near-Infrared Fluorescence Imaging with Indocyanine Green for Intraoperative Detection of Canine Urothelial Carcinoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/646)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. This study looks at whether a fluorescent dye, indocyanine green, viewed with near-infrared imaging, helps surgeons detect urothelial carcinoma during an operation. It tests a surgical imaging method rather than a new cancer drug. The listing says it is for dogs with bladder tumors (urothelial carcinoma) that require surgical treatment. Because complete surgical removal is unlikely for most bladder TCC ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)), this study fits a narrower group of dogs. The database says full coverage, but CSU covers the dye/imaging and provides a surgery credit. Owners pay diagnosis, surgery beyond the credit, hospitalization and unrelated care. Its current criteria require a surgically removable tumor, no spread beyond the bladder and no prior tumor treatment other than NSAIDs. Confirm with the team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/near-infrared-fluorescence-imaging-with-indocyanine-green-for-intraoperative-detection-of-canine-urothelial-carcinoma/)

### A related prostate cancer listing

TCC can spread through the prostate as well as the ureters, bladder and urethra ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats); [Purdue](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)). The study below is listed for prostate cancer. Neither the listing nor Penn Vet's page mentions TCC or urothelial carcinoma, so whether a dog whose cancer involves the prostate could qualify is a question for the study team and your oncologist.

### [PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer](https://vettrials.org/trial/32)

University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine (Penn Vet), Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The study is assessing an investigational targeted agent, PSMA-MMAE-Pc413, combined with laser therapy, for local and metastatic prostate cancer in dogs. Penn Vet's page did not state a current enrollment status when we checked. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Penn Vet's page says the study covers the infusions, laser, sedation and recheck visits. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/clinical-trial/psma-ligand-based-theranostic-to-treat-canine-prostatic-cancer/)

## Finding clinical trials for dogs with bladder cancer: other places to look

The four listings above are what the VetTrials recruiting search returned on November 3, 2026. A few other leads are worth knowing about.

- Purdue University's own bladder cancer trials page (last updated July 30, 2026) listed an "Immunotherapy Trial for Dogs with Urinary Bladder Cancer" as actively recruiting when we checked. It did not appear in the VetTrials recruiting results that day. The page asks for no prior radiation or chemotherapy, requires treatment and monitoring at the Purdue University Veterinary Hospital, and states that owners pay $300 per visit while the study covers the remaining hospital costs. Read the full criteria on [Purdue's trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php).
- VetTrials also carries bladder tumor listings whose recruiting status the source does not state. They are left off the list above, but you can see them by [searching without the recruiting filter](https://vettrials.org/?q=bladder&species=dog) and confirming status with each institution.
- Some studies accept several kinds of solid tumors rather than one cancer type. Our guide to dog cancer clinical trials covers those broader studies, and our dog cancer vaccine guide covers vaccine and immunotherapy studies.

## What joining a bladder cancer trial can involve

Details vary, but the study pages give a realistic picture. NC State's study involves treatment under general anesthesia on day one, about three days in the hospital, outpatient checks on days 4 and 8, repeated blood and urine samples, and quality-of-life questionnaires ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)). Purdue's study starts with a two-day visit that includes x-rays, ultrasound and a cystoscopy under anesthesia, gives IV treatments at the hospital every two weeks, and asks owners to consent to a necropsy (an after-death examination) when the dog eventually dies ([Purdue trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)).

Expect rules about other medicines. Purdue requires a break from NSAIDs and supplements before enrollment and excludes dogs receiving Librela or Cytopoint ([Purdue trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)). NC State allows NSAIDs but not prednisone or other immunotherapy ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)). Do not stop or change any medication on your own; talk with your veterinarian first.

Cost coverage is rarely all or nothing. Some studies pay for the study treatment but not routine care at your regular clinic, and Purdue notes that once a dog leaves the study, further treatment is billed at full price ([Purdue trials page](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)). Our guide to the cost of chemotherapy for dogs can help you compare a trial with standard treatment.

## What "recruiting" means here

"Recruiting" on this page means recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. It does not establish the institution's current enrollment status. It is not a promise that a spot is open today. Studies fill, pause and close, sometimes faster than their web pages are updated, and an institution may be screening only certain dogs. Treat the label as a reason to call, then confirm status and eligibility directly with the study team and your veterinarian.

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how soon could my dog be screened?
- What diagnosis do you need: biopsy, cytology, a urine BRAF test?
- Does tumor location (bladder neck, urethra, prostate) or spread affect eligibility?
- Which past or current treatments, including NSAIDs and supplements, rule a dog out, and is a washout period needed?
- What exactly does the study pay for, and what will I pay, including travel and care at my own clinic?
- How many visits, nights in the hospital and anesthetic procedures are involved?
- What happens if side effects appear or the cancer grows during the study?
- Can my dog keep seeing our regular veterinarian, and will you share results with them?

## Sources

- [Neoplasia of the Urinary System in Dogs and Cats, Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/urinary-system/noninfectious-diseases-of-the-urinary-system-in-small-animals/neoplasia-of-the-urinary-system-in-dogs-and-cats)
- [Canine Urinary Bladder Cancer Research, Purdue University College of Veterinary Medicine](https://www.vet.purdue.edu/pcop/urinary-bladder-cancer-research.php)
- [Urinary Bladder Cancer Trials for Dogs, Purdue University College of Veterinary Medicine](https://vet.purdue.edu/wcorc/clinical-trials/canine-urinary-bladder-cancer.php)
- [Now Enrolling Dogs with Invasive Bladder Cancer, NC State College of Veterinary Medicine](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)
- [PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer, Penn Vet](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/clinical-trial/psma-ligand-based-theranostic-to-treat-canine-prostatic-cancer/)

body:
If your dog has just been diagnosed with osteosarcoma, this page lists the canine osteosarcoma clinical trials labeled recruiting in the VetTrials trial database snapshot checked November 3, 2026, for dogs in the United States and Canada. Each entry says what the study is looking at, where it runs, the main eligibility point we could see, and how the listing describes cost coverage.

The most useful next step is simple: share this list with your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist, and contact any study team that looks relevant as early as you can. Many of these studies have timing rules tied to amputation, chemotherapy or radiation, and some can only accept a dog before one of those steps happens. You can also run the [live osteosarcoma search](https://vettrials.org/?q=osteosarcoma&species=dog&status=recruiting) at any time for the current list.

## Osteosarcoma in dogs, in plain words

Osteosarcoma is a bone cancer. The Merck Veterinary Manual describes it as the most common primary bone tumor in dogs, accounting for over 80% of canine bone tumors ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteopathies-in-small-animals/bone-tumors-in-dogs-and-cats)). A 2025 consensus guideline lists breed, size and age as risk factors ([Polton et al., Frontiers in Veterinary Science, 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)), and NCI describes it as a cancer that develops in large-breed dogs ([NCI Cancer Currents](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)).

Owners often first notice lameness or a swelling on a leg. Merck lists lameness, bone swelling and a fracture without an injury as signs of bone tumors, and notes that a bone biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis, with chest X-rays used to look for spread ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteopathies-in-small-animals/bone-tumors-in-dogs-and-cats)).

Two terms show up in almost every trial listing:

- **Appendicular** means the tumor is in a limb (the "appendicular skeleton" is the legs). Most canine osteosarcomas start there ([Poon et al., Canadian Veterinary Journal, 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7020630/)).
- **Metastatic** means the cancer has spread beyond the original bone. In dogs the lungs are the main place veterinarians look for spread, which is why chest X-rays are part of staging ([Polton et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)). Researchers estimate that most dogs already have microscopic spread at diagnosis that X-rays cannot yet show ([Poon et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7020630/)).

This is why trial listings so often say "no evidence of metastasis" or, the opposite, "metastatic osteosarcoma." They are written for dogs at different points in the disease.

## How it is usually treated

The Canadian Veterinary Journal review describes amputation of the affected limb followed by chemotherapy as the current standard of care ([Poon et al., 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7020630/)). The 2025 consensus guideline names carboplatin as the single-agent chemotherapy of choice after surgery and says chemotherapy should start shortly after, or at the time of, amputation ([Polton et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)).

Limb-sparing surgery removes the tumor but keeps the leg. The same guideline describes it as appropriate for a minority of cases, mainly early-stage tumors of the distal radius (the end of the forearm bone near the wrist), and says limb-preserving surgery has not been shown to produce better survival than amputation ([Polton et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)). Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT, a few high-precision radiation doses) is another way to treat the tumor without amputation; the guideline notes that bone fractures after SBRT have been its main complication ([Polton et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)).

Pain control matters at every stage. Merck lists anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids and radiation therapy as palliative options to ease bone pain ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteopathies-in-small-animals/bone-tumors-in-dogs-and-cats)). Which path fits a particular dog is a conversation for your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist.

## Why timing matters when you look at trials

Most osteosarcoma studies are designed around one moment in treatment, so the order of events can decide whether a dog is eligible. Reading the listings below, you will see three broad groups:

- **Leg still present.** Several studies only accept dogs whose affected leg has not been amputated, and some require no previous surgery, radiation or chemotherapy for the tumor.
- **Around amputation.** Some studies need to be arranged before surgery, or need the amputation done at the study hospital so tumor tissue can be collected.
- **After spread to the lungs.** A few studies are only for dogs whose cancer has already spread, often after amputation and chemotherapy are finished.

We are not suggesting you delay or change any treatment. The point is practical: if a study interests you, contact the study team before the next big step (biopsy, amputation, the first chemotherapy dose or radiation) so they can tell you whether that step affects eligibility, and talk it through with your veterinarian or oncologist.

## Canine osteosarcoma trials listed as recruiting (checked November 3, 2026)

Each study below is listed as recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. That database label is not confirmation that the institution is currently enrolling. Recruiting status can change quickly, so confirm with the institution before planning anything. VetTrials is an independent listing site. It is not the enrolling institution and is not affiliated with AVMA's veterinaryclinicaltrials.org registry or with any of the universities listed. Eligibility is decided by each study team.

**Studies for dogs that have not had amputation or other treatment for the tumor.** Most of these ask for the leg to still be in place.

### [The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/608)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. This study is looking at whether a single dose of the chemotherapy drug carboplatin, given into a vein, affects pain, measured by how well dogs walk, how active they are and how they sleep. The institution page asks for dogs with the leg still present, no previous chemotherapy or radiation, and no sign that the cancer has spread to other bones. The database labels coverage full, but cSU covers specified tests, one carboplatin dose and rechecks; baseline pain medicine and additional side-effect care can be owner-paid. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/the-effect-of-intravenous-carboplatin-on-pain-control-in-dogs-with-appendicular-osteosarcoma/)

### [Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy](https://vettrials.org/trial/434)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. An observational study: dogs that are already going to receive SBRT followed by carboplatin have extra CT scans and blood and urine samples to track bone breakdown and fracture risk. The institution page asks for no fracture caused by the tumor, no spread, and no previous radiation. The owner pays for the radiation and chemotherapy themselves; the study pays for its extra tests. The database labels coverage full, but cSU says owners pay standard radiation, chemotherapy and other care; the study pays extra tests and contributes toward radiation. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/dual-energy-ct-to-assess-bone-mineral-density-in-dogs-with-osteosarcoma-undergoing-stereotacticbody-radiation-therapy/)

### [3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor](https://vettrials.org/trial/647)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. This study is evaluating limb-sparing surgery that replaces the diseased bone with a custom 3D-printed implant, followed by chemotherapy and long-term monitoring. The listing is for giant breed dogs, and the institution page asks about tumors in the wrist area (distal radius) with the leg still present. The database labels coverage full, but cSU covers major study costs, but owners pay initial testing, outside visits and complications beyond the study allowance. Eligible dogs are giant breed or at least 40 kg. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/3d-printed-implant-that-replaces-bone-for-limb-sparing-in-giant-breed-dogs-with-a-primary-bone-tumor/)

### [Evaluating a Non-Invasive Heat Therapy for the Treatment of Bone Cancer in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/304)

Ontario Veterinary College, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario. A pilot study of MRI-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), which uses focused sound energy to heat and destroy tumor tissue without surgery. The listing asks for confirmed osteosarcoma of the distal radius, no evidence of spread and no previous surgery or radiation for the tumor; prior chemotherapy or bisphosphonate treatment is considered case by case. The institution page notes visits to a Toronto hospital as well as to Guelph. Cost coverage noted in the listing: partial. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/evaluating-a-non-invasive-heat-therapy-for-the-treatment-of-bone-cancer-in-dogs-2/)

### [Evaluating Effects of a new Bone Tumor Treatment](https://vettrials.org/trial/39)

Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine, Blacksburg, Virginia. The study evaluates histotripsy, a technique that destroys tissue without radiation or heat, combined with an immune-stimulating drug. Read the institution page closely: it says the treatment portion has completed and the team is still seeking dogs for the control group, which receives standard amputation and chemotherapy. Dogs need no lung spread on chest X-rays and no previous cancer treatment. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.vt.edu/clinical-trials/current-studies/histotripsy-osteo-no-amputation.html)

### [Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial](https://vettrials.org/trial/487)

Johns Hopkins University, Center for Image-Guided Animal Therapy (CIGAT), Baltimore, Maryland. The listing asks for dogs of any breed, sex and age with biopsy-confirmed osteosarcoma of a limb, otherwise healthy, with no prior treatment for osteosarcoma and no chemotherapy for other cancers. Owners need to be able to bring the dog to Baltimore for treatment and follow-up. Johns Hopkins’ own page says this tests cryotherapy or investigational immunotherapy before required amputation and chemotherapy. It labels the trial open and enrolling. Study treatment and specified imaging are covered, but amputation and chemotherapy are not. [Institution page](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/radiology/veterinarians/clinical-trials#osteosarcoma) Cost coverage noted in the listing: partial. Confirm with the study team.

**Studies built around amputation, chemotherapy or radiation.** Several need to be arranged before surgery or radiation begins.

### [Amputation and Chemotherapy for Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/40)

Virginia-Maryland College of Veterinary Medicine, Blacksburg, Virginia. For dogs whose owners have already chosen standard care (amputation, then chemotherapy). Dogs are monitored with bloodwork and chest X-rays to see if and when the cancer spreads, as a comparison group for other trials. The institution page asks owners or their veterinarian to get in touch before the amputation, and excludes dogs with lung spread on chest X-rays. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated (the institution page describes a credit toward surgery or chemotherapy and covered follow-up X-rays). Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.vt.edu/clinical-trials/current-studies/amputation-and-chemotherapy-for-osteosarcoma.html)

### [Vaccine Study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/145)

University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida. An investigational vaccine given alongside standard chemotherapy. The institution page says dogs must be newly diagnosed and untreated, and become eligible once the affected limb has been amputated and sampled at the University of Florida, so contact the team before surgery elsewhere. The same page says costs, including the vaccines, are the owner's responsibility. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-osteosarcoma/)

### [mRNA Vaccine Study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/146)

University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida. This study tests an RNA nanoparticle vaccine made from each dog's own tumor cells, given with an anti-PD1 immunotherapy drug, in dogs that are receiving radiation therapy. The institution page says tumor cells must be collected before radiation starts, and that dogs with mild spread may be considered at the investigator's discretion. It describes the study covering vaccine-related costs while owners pay for standard diagnosis and radiation. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/mrna-vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-appendicular-osteosarcoma-currently-enrolling/)

**Studies for dogs whose cancer has spread to the lungs.**

### [CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/436)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado. CAR T cell therapy takes some of the dog's own immune cells (T cells) from a blood sample, modifies them in a lab to recognize cancer cells, and gives them back by IV. The institution page asks for dogs whose leg tumor has been removed, with spread only to the lungs on chest X-rays, weighing at least 44 lb (20 kg), and with no chemotherapy in the past two to three weeks. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full (the institution page notes owners pay the initial workup and exam fees). Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/car-t-cell-immunotherapy-for-treatment-of-metastatic-osteosarcoma-in-dogs/)

### [Cell Therapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/31)

University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. A study of engineered immune cells called CAR-iNKT cells in dogs whose osteosarcoma has spread to the lungs, looking first at safety and dose. The institution page describes the cells as made from a healthy donor dog's blood, and lists amputation followed by carboplatin, a tumor that tests positive for a marker called B7-H3, and a body weight of at least 18 kg among its requirements. That page does not state whether enrollment is open today. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated (the institution page says treatment costs are covered). Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/clinical-trial/cell-therapy-for-metastatic-osteosarcoma/)

## Why dogs with osteosarcoma are studied so closely

Osteosarcoma develops in both large-breed dogs and young people, and NCI researchers have described the genetic features of the disease in dogs and humans as so similar that they are hard to tell apart ([NCI Cancer Currents](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)). NCI's Comparative Oncology Program works with a network of veterinary schools across the United States and Canada to run trials in pet dogs with naturally occurring cancer, and NCI notes that its funded trials typically offer substantial, if not complete, financial support for the cost of care ([NCI Cancer Currents](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)). That shared interest is one reason so many of the studies above test new immune therapies and imaging tools.

For a wider view of cancer studies in dogs, see our guide to dog cancer clinical trials. If the vaccine studies above caught your eye, our dog cancer vaccine guide explains what those studies are and are not.

## What joining a study usually involves, and what it costs

Expect a screening visit first: records review, an exam, bloodwork and imaging such as chest X-rays, sometimes a biopsy. Several institution pages above say the screening visit is not always covered, even when the treatment is. After enrollment, most studies need repeat visits on a fixed schedule at the study hospital, which can mean travel.

"Full" or "partial" coverage in a listing rarely means every bill is paid. Read the cost section of the institution page and ask for a written list of what the study pays for, what you pay for, and what happens if your dog has a side effect. Our guide to dog chemotherapy costs can help you compare a study with standard care.

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how soon could my dog be screened?
- Does the timing of amputation, biopsy, chemotherapy or radiation affect eligibility?
- Which current medications (for example pain medicines or bisphosphonates) are not allowed?
- What does the study pay for, and what will I pay for, including screening and side effects?
- How many visits are needed, over how long, and can any happen with my own veterinarian?
- What standard treatment will my dog still receive, and can we leave the study at any time?
- Who do I call after hours if something goes wrong?

## What "recruiting" means on this page

"Recruiting" on this page means recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. It does not establish the institution's current enrollment status. It does not mean your dog qualifies, and it can change without notice when a study fills or closes. Some institution pages are updated less often than others, so always confirm current enrollment directly with the institution and your veterinarian. You can learn more about how this site works on the [About VetTrials](https://vettrials.org/about) page.

## Sources

- [Bone Tumors in Dogs and Cats, Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteopathies-in-small-animals/bone-tumors-in-dogs-and-cats)
- [Osteosarcoma of the appendicular skeleton in dogs: consensus and guidelines, Frontiers in Veterinary Science (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12498955/)
- [Recent and current clinical trials in canine appendicular osteosarcoma, Canadian Veterinary Journal (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7020630/)
- [Helping Dogs and Humans with Cancer: NCI's Comparative Oncology Studies, National Cancer Institute](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)

body:
If your dog has just been diagnosed with cancer, this page groups canine cancer clinical trials labeled recruiting in the VetTrials trial database by cancer type. The database snapshot checked November 3, 2026 contains 53 listings across 15 institutions in the United States and Canada, covering lymphoma, bone cancer, bladder cancer, melanoma, brain tumors and more.

Find your dog's cancer type below, open the listings that fit, and bring them to your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist. They can tell you whether a study is worth a call, and the study team decides who qualifies. For the newest results, use the [live dog cancer trial search](https://vettrials.org/?condition=oncology&species=dog&status=recruiting).

## Why dogs with cancer join clinical trials

A clinical trial tests a new or existing treatment, device or diagnostic test in patients with a naturally occurring illness, after laboratory work has supported studying it further ([NC State College of Veterinary Medicine](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)). Cancer trials at veterinary schools evaluate new drugs, new uses for older drugs, and new approaches to surgery or radiation therapy ([Colorado State University Flint Animal Cancer Center](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trials/)).

For an owner, the possible upsides are access to a treatment before it is widely available and expert care during the study. Some trials also cover part or all of the cost of care, testing or treatment ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)). The same source is clear about the other side: the experimental treatment may not work for your dog, it may cause side effects, and a trial can mean more visits than usual care ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)). Taking part also contributes to medical research ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)), and Colorado State describes each trial patient as providing information that helps improve care for future patients, both pets and people ([Colorado State](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trials/)).

Not every listing below is a treatment study. Some collect blood or tissue, compare imaging methods, or follow dogs getting standard care. Read each listing's title closely so you know which kind of study you are looking at.

## How comparative oncology connects dogs and people

Comparative oncology uses naturally occurring cancers in pet dogs to learn more about cancer in both dogs and people. NCI describes shared features in how cancers grow, spread and respond to the immune system, and explains how dog studies can inform human drug development ([NCI, comparative oncology](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)).

NCI’s 2019 overview describes a network of veterinary schools in the United States and Canada working on canine cancer studies. It says NCI-supported trials are reviewed for animal welfare and scientific merit and typically offer substantial financial support. Those statements describe the NCI program, not every listing below ([NCI](https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2019/comparative-oncology-dogs-cancer-clinical-trials)).

You will see this connection in the list below. Missouri’s current clinical-trials page describes COTC033 and says it is enrolling dogs with eligible solid tumors ([University of Missouri](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)). Many other listings are single-site studies funded by companies, foundations or grants ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)).

## What joining a trial involves

A practical first step is to ask your veterinarian to contact the study team named on the institution's page. Many listings above set firm rules, like weight ranges, tumor size, cancer stage, or no prior chemotherapy, so have your dog's diagnosis, imaging and bloodwork records ready, and ask whether a screening visit is needed before the team can confirm a fit.

Before enrolling, you will be asked to sign an informed consent document that explains the study's requirements and risks. NC State notes that informed consent is not a contract, and you can withdraw from a trial at any time ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)). A 2024 review of veterinary consent practice says a good consent form describes the study's goals, lists all risks of taking part, explains the owner's responsibilities, details any compensation, and tells owners they will be informed of significant new findings that affect the study ([Frederick, Frontiers in Veterinary Science](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11231070/)). At NC State, trials at the teaching hospital must also be approved by the university's animal care and use committee ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)).

A trial may require more visits than standard care. Some studies need rechecks, scans or blood draws on a set schedule, and most sites on this page are university hospitals that may be a long drive away. Ask about the schedule before you commit.

## Costs and cost coverage

Funding for veterinary trials comes from many places, including national grants, foundations and private companies ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/research/clinical-trials/)). That is why coverage varies so much from one listing to the next. A label of "full" does not tell you exactly which costs are covered, and "not stated" only means the listing did not say. Ask the study team to spell out, in writing, what is and is not covered. For what standard cancer treatment can cost outside a trial, see our guide to dog chemotherapy costs.

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how many dogs are you still looking for?
- What does my dog need to qualify, and which records or tests do you need from my veterinarian?
- What is being tested, and is there a comparison group or placebo?
- Which costs does the study cover, which are mine, and what happens if my dog has a side effect?
- How many visits are required, how often, and for how long?
- Can my dog keep taking current medications or receive other treatment during the study?
- What happens if I decide to stop, or if the cancer progresses?
- Will you share results with me and my veterinarian?

## What "recruiting" means on this page

"Recruiting" on this page means recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 3, 2026. It does not establish the institution's current enrollment status. Studies fill, pause and close, and pages are not always updated the same day, so the label can be out of date. Always confirm with the study team, and ask your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist whether a trial makes sense for your dog. You can read more about how listings are collected on our [about page](https://vettrials.org/about), and the [live search](https://vettrials.org/?condition=oncology&species=dog&status=recruiting) shows the current list.

title: Dog Chemo Cost: What Drives It and When Trials Help Pay
heading: Dog Chemo Cost: When a Clinical Trial Can Help Pay
description: How much does chemo for dogs cost? What drives the bill, fees teaching hospitals publish, and 21 recruiting dog cancer trials noting cost coverage.

cta.heading: Look for a study that may cover part of the cost
cta.text: Search dog cancer studies listed as recruiting, then confirm cost coverage and eligibility with the study team and your veterinarian.

body:
There is no single price for chemotherapy in dogs. What you pay depends on the type of cancer, the treatment plan your oncologist recommends, your dog's size, and where the care happens. Below we explain those cost factors using university veterinary sources, show the few dollar figures that teaching hospitals publish themselves (with dates), and list the recruiting dog cancer studies whose listings note full or partial cost coverage.

We checked this page on November 1, 2026. If cost is shaping your decision, two good next steps are to ask your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist for a written estimate, and to [search recruiting dog cancer trials](https://vettrials.org/?condition=oncology&species=dog&status=recruiting) to see whether a study near you might cover part of the care.

## How much does chemo for dogs cost? What drives the bill

Cornell University's College of Veterinary Medicine says the cost of evaluation, diagnosis, staging and treatment varies with the site of the tumor, the size of the dog, the treatment selected and how well the dog handles treatment. Cornell says chemotherapy costs vary with the size of the dog and may run from several hundred dollars for palliative oral treatment to several thousand dollars over a three-to-six-month period ([Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, Cancer Management FAQ, page undated, checked November 1, 2026](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/node/2940)). That is a wide range on purpose: the plan itself sets the price.

Here are the pieces that usually add up to the total. Apart from Cornell's broad ranges, we have not attached dollar amounts to them, because we could not find university or AVMA sources that publish current prices for each one.

- **Diagnosis and staging.** Before treatment, a dog usually needs tests to confirm the cancer type and see whether it has spread. Cornell says diagnosis, staging and consultation may range from several hundred dollars upward, more if the tumor is in a body cavity or otherwise hard to reach ([Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/node/2940)).
- **The protocol and number of visits.** A protocol is the schedule of drugs and visits. The Merck Veterinary Manual says the choice of protocol depends on the tumor type, its grade and stage, the dog's overall condition, financial considerations and the goals of treatment ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/pharmacology/antineoplastic-agents/overview-of-antineoplastic-agents)). A short palliative plan and a months-long multi-drug plan cost very different amounts.
- **Drug choice.** Oral drugs given at home and injectable drugs given in the hospital carry different drug, handling and visit costs. Cornell's range runs from oral palliative treatment at the low end to multi-month courses at the high end ([Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/node/2940)).
- **Your dog's size.** Many chemotherapy doses are calculated from body surface area, and small dogs are often dosed by weight ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/pharmacology/antineoplastic-agents/overview-of-antineoplastic-agents)). Bigger dogs need more drug, and Cornell notes chemotherapy costs vary with the size of the dog ([Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/node/2940)).
- **Monitoring bloodwork.** Merck recommends baseline lab values before treatment and routine complete blood counts timed to when white blood cell counts are expected to be lowest ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/pharmacology/antineoplastic-agents/overview-of-antineoplastic-agents)). Each of those checks is a line on the bill.
- **Side-effect care.** Cornell lists the most common side effects as stomach upset, reduced appetite, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Cornell describes them as generally mild and self-limiting, but says they may need treatment or hospitalization in some cases ([Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/node/2940)). Ask whether anti-nausea medicine and urgent visits are included in an estimate.
- **Referral hospital or general practice, and region.** Some chemotherapy is given by a specialty or university oncology service and some by a general practice working with an oncologist. Fees differ between hospitals and parts of the country, so an estimate from one clinic does not predict another's.

## One published fee from a teaching hospital

Most university hospitals do not post chemotherapy prices, because every plan is customized. One that does publish a starting fee is Colorado State University's Flint Animal Cancer Center. Its FAQ lists a specialty fee of $278.00 for the new patient visit, plus a $15.00 environmental cleaning fee, and says that visit includes detailed estimates for diagnostics and treatment ([Colorado State University Flint Animal Cancer Center FAQ, page undated, checked November 1, 2026](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/faq/)). That is the consultation only, not treatment, and it applies to that hospital.

The [AVMA](https://www.avma.org/resources-tools/pet-owners/petcare/financial-assistance-veterinary-care-costs) groups chemotherapy with other unexpected care such as diagnostic tests, surgery and hospital stays, and encourages owners to talk openly with their veterinarian about cost, since a range of care options is often available.

## How clinical trials can help pay

A veterinary clinical trial is a study in pet dogs with a naturally occurring disease, run by a university or specialty hospital to answer a research question. Because the study needs the data, it often pays for some of the care involved. The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center says there are often financial reasons to enroll, that it is often able to subsidize the cost of treatment once a pet qualifies, and that in many cases owners pay for the initial evaluation, and pre-enrollment tests may be the owner's responsibility ([University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center, Oncology Clinical Trials](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/)).

What "covered" means changes from study to study. Missouri's current trials page, checked November 1, 2026, shows the range in its own words ([University of Missouri, Current Clinical Trials](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)):

- One lymphoma study says all treatments and rechecks are covered, including initial staging, with up to $4,000 set aside for possible adverse events and a $2,000 stipend toward additional or future treatment at the hospital once the study is complete.
- A lung cancer study covers the study drug, which the page prices at $540 to $1,350 per treatment depending on patient size, while the owner pays for recheck exams, bloodwork and X-rays.
- A thyroid study contributes $1,500 toward clinical costs after enrollment, while the full screening before enrollment is at the owner's expense.

So a study listed as "fully funded" and one listed as "partially funded" can both leave you with some costs, and the gap is usually in screening, travel, follow-up care or treatment for side effects. Joining a study also means following its visit schedule, and the treatment being tested may not work. A trial is one option to raise with your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist, alongside standard treatment.

## Dog cancer trials noting cost coverage (checked November 1, 2026)

On November 1, 2026, VetTrials showed 53 dog cancer listings labeled as recruiting. Of those, 21 noted full or partial cost coverage, listed below. The other 32 did not state funding, which does not mean they are unpaid; it means you need to ask.

Each study below is listed as recruiting by its source. The cost label comes from the listing and may cover only study-related costs, so confirm what is included, and whether the study is still enrolling, with the study team. VetTrials is an independent listing site. It is not the enrolling institution and is not affiliated with the AVMA's registry or with any of the universities listed. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether any of these fit your dog.

### Listings that note full cost coverage

- [The Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/608), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/436), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy](https://vettrials.org/trial/434), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy](https://vettrials.org/trial/355), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Combination of Lapatinib and Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Transitional Cell Carcinoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/432), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Minimally invasive sentinel lymph node mapping for canine apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)](https://vettrials.org/trial/648), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor](https://vettrials.org/trial/647), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Pilot Clinical Trial of Trametinib Treatment in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)](https://vettrials.org/trial/565), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Near-Infrared Fluorescence Imaging with Indocyanine Green for Intraoperative Detection of Canine Urothelial Carcinoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/646), Colorado State University, Fort Collins CO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Canine Brain Cancer Clinical Trial (Radiation Therapy Combined with Chemotherapy In Dogs with Brain Tumors)](https://vettrials.org/trial/655), Johns Hopkins University (CIGAT), Baltimore MD. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [LEAH xCAR-T: Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/65), University of Missouri, Columbia MO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers](https://vettrials.org/trial/60), University of Missouri, Columbia MO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/329), University of Missouri, Columbia MO. Cost coverage noted: full.
- [Become a Canine Cancer Hero](https://vettrials.org/trial/93), NC State University, Raleigh NC. Cost coverage noted: full. This is a tissue donation program, not a treatment study: tumor tissue is donated after a dog's death for research, and NC State's own page currently describes it for dogs with primary lung cancer and does not state what costs are covered.

### Listings that note partial cost coverage

- [Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial](https://vettrials.org/trial/487), Johns Hopkins University (CIGAT), Baltimore MD. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Evaluating a Non-Invasive Heat Therapy for the Treatment of Bone Cancer in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/304), Ontario Veterinary College (University of Guelph), Guelph, Ontario, Canada. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Can We Use a Mobile App to Measure Oral Tumours in Dogs?](https://vettrials.org/trial/301), Ontario Veterinary College (University of Guelph), Guelph, Ontario, Canada. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Evaluating Palladia® for the Treatment of Canine Oral Melanoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/299), Ontario Veterinary College (University of Guelph), Guelph, Ontario, Canada. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Pilot Study Evaluating the Microbiota in Dogs with Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/274), Oregon State University, Corvallis OR. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Thyroid Sodium Iodide Symporter](https://vettrials.org/trial/67), University of Missouri, Columbia MO. Cost coverage noted: partial.
- [Gilvetmab for the Treatment of Primary Pulmonary Carcinoma in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/64), University of Missouri, Columbia MO. Cost coverage noted: partial.

For more detail by cancer type, see our guides to dog cancer clinical trials, canine lymphoma clinical trials and canine osteosarcoma clinical trials.

## What "recruiting" means on this page

"Recruiting" is the label the source institution gave the study when VetTrials last checked it. Studies fill up, pause or close without notice, and eligibility rules are stricter than a one-line listing can show. Treat the label as a reason to call, not a guarantee of a spot. You can read more about how listings are gathered on our [about page](https://vettrials.org/about).

## Questions to ask a study team about costs

Ask for answers in writing before you enroll. Missouri's own clinical trials page suggests "What are the costs?" as a question every owner should ask ([University of Missouri](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/)).

- What exactly does the study pay for: the study drug, exams, imaging, bloodwork, hospital stays?
- What is not covered? Who pays for screening tests done before my dog is accepted?
- If my dog has side effects, does the study pay for that care, and is there a limit?
- How many visits are required, over how long, and are follow-up visits after treatment covered?
- Does the study help with travel or lodging if we live far away?
- What happens to costs if my dog leaves the study early, whether by my choice, because the disease progresses, or because the team ends participation?
- Is there any credit toward standard treatment after the study ends?
- Can my regular veterinarian handle some of the monitoring closer to home?

## Other ways owners look for help paying

The AVMA's page for pet owners on managing veterinary costs suggests talking openly with your veterinarian about a care plan that fits your budget, and asking about payment plans, deferred payments and financing, which not every clinic offers. It notes that some veterinary schools and nonprofit organizations may offer financial assistance to owners who can show need, and that crowdfunding is another route ([AVMA, Loving your pet, managing the costs](https://www.avma.org/resources-tools/pet-owners/petcare/financial-assistance-veterinary-care-costs)).

The same AVMA page keeps a list of organizations that may help, including a section on cancer treatment support. The AVMA says it does not endorse any specific program, and it advises checking each organization's website for current eligibility rules and asking your local veterinary medical association or humane organization about local resources ([AVMA](https://www.avma.org/resources-tools/pet-owners/petcare/financial-assistance-veterinary-care-costs)).
