body:
This page lists dog arthritis clinical trials that were marked as recruiting when we checked on November 3, 2026: six studies at five veterinary schools and hospitals in New York, North Carolina, Tennessee and Ontario. They test supplements, a collar, joint injections and a pain procedure for osteoarthritis, the gradual breakdown of joint cartilage that leads to stiffness and limping ([Merck Veterinary Manual](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/dog-owners/bone,-joint,-and-muscle-disorders-of-dogs/osteoarthritis-degenerative-joint-disease)).

The six listings below are a starting point, and most of this page is a practical guide to applying: what these studies usually ask for, how to get your dog's records ready, and what to ask the study team. The short version: talk with your veterinarian first, then contact the team named on the institution's page. You can also [search current arthritis listings](https://vettrials.org/?q=arthritis&species=dog&status=recruiting) at any time.

## Dog arthritis trials listed as recruiting (checked November 3, 2026)

Each study below is labeled recruiting in the VetTrials database checked November 3, 2026. That label does not confirm the institution is enrolling today. Status can change without notice, so confirm with the institution before you plan a visit. VetTrials is an [independent listing site](https://vettrials.org/about). It is not the enrolling institution, and it is not affiliated with the AVMA's registry or with any of the universities or hospitals listed here.

### Supplement and diet studies

Three studies look at something a dog eats. Visit schedules vary. These studies may ask you to keep diet and other supplements steady for weeks or months.

### [Seal Oil and Salmon Oil for the Treatment of Osteoarthritis](https://vettrials.org/trial/310)

Ontario Veterinary College, University of Guelph, in Guelph, Ontario (Canada). This nutrition study looks at marine oil supplements (seal oil, with salmon oil named in the title) for dogs with osteoarthritis. The institution’s current page accepts dogs over 4 years old and over 11 kg (25 lb), whether intact or neutered, with confirmed osteoarthritis or clinical lameness in at least one limb, who eat a commercial dry kibble diet. The database’s older 20 kg and neutering restrictions are out of date. It describes two visits and an online screening survey. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution's page lists the exam, X-rays, blood work, urinalysis, kibble and oil supplement as study-covered. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/seal-oil-for-the-treatment-of-osteoarthritis/) The institution page does not explicitly confirm current enrollment; ask the team before planning a visit.

### [Seeking Dogs with Arthritis for a Joint Supplement Study](https://vettrials.org/trial/316)

Animal Medical Center, New York, New York (Manhattan). The hospital's sports medicine and rehabilitation team is running a joint supplement study, and a dog may receive a placebo during the study (the supplement is offered at the end in that case). The institution's page asks for dogs at least 3 years old, 10 to 100 lb, with signs of arthritis such as limping or trouble with stairs, X-ray confirmation, and no other unstable disease. It lists exclusions, including recent steroid use, recent joint injections, recent joint surgery, and a Librela injection in the last 2 months. The study runs about 90 days with two in-person visits and three phone check-ins. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution's page lists free exams, blood and urine tests, gait analysis and the supplement, plus a payment to owners who complete the study. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)

### [GI Supplement Clinical Study](https://vettrials.org/trial/450)

NC State College of Veterinary Medicine, Raleigh, North Carolina. The institution says dogs with osteoarthritis or mobility problems are being enrolled to study the connection between gut health and joint disease. The institution's page describes a double-blind trial of a prebiotic supplement and its effect on pain, with visits that include imaging and walking and standing measurements. It offers a short online questionnaire and an information call to check fit. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution's page lists free exams, lab work and X-rays and gift cards on completion. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/gi-supplement-clinical-study/)

### Device, injection and procedure studies

These three studies involve a device or a procedure and more frequent rechecks. Two of them, both at Tennessee, randomly assign dogs to different groups.

### [Collar for Lameness and Osteoarthritis in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/3)

University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine, Knoxville, Tennessee. Dogs are randomly assigned to a collar containing an active blend, which the study team describes as intended to be absorbed through the skin, or to a placebo collar. The study flyer asks for dogs 1 to 8 years old, 15 to 40 kg, with X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis in a shoulder, elbow, hip or knee, plus lameness. It excludes dogs receiving pain medicines other than an NSAID or gabapentin, and asks that dogs not receive joint supplements for 4 weeks before the start. Rechecks happen every 2 weeks for 8 weeks, with gait measurements on a force plate, blood samples and owner questionnaires. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The flyer says study expenses, including X-rays and blood work, are covered and describes an honorarium for completing the study. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf) The flyer is dated September 2024 and gives no current enrollment status; ask the team before planning a visit.

### [Intra-Articular Polymer Beads for Hip Dysplasia in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/6)

University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine, Knoxville, Tennessee. This study is for dogs with moderate hip osteoarthritis caused by hip dysplasia. Dogs are randomly assigned to a hip injection of hyaluronic acid, soft polymer beads, or both, given under sedation and local anesthetic with a small camera to guide the needle. The flyer asks for dogs 1 to 8 years old and 15 to 40 kg, and excludes dogs with other orthopedic problems such as a torn cruciate ligament or a slipping kneecap. Assessments happen every 2 weeks for 8 weeks and again at 4 months, with owner questionnaires. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The flyer says study expenses are covered and describes an honorarium for completion. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Intra-Articular-Polymer-Beads-for-Hip-Dysplasia.pdf) The flyer is dated September 2024 and gives no current enrollment status; ask the team before planning a visit.

### [Radiofrequency Therapy for Pain Management in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/80)

Cornell University Hospital for Animals, Ithaca, New York. The institution's page describes this study as being for dogs seen at the hospital with knee (stifle) arthritis pain that is hard to control with other treatments. Dogs walk across a pressure-sensing mat, then have a radiofrequency procedure under sedation or anesthesia and can go home the same day. Follow-up walks and an owner questionnaire happen at 2 weeks, 4 weeks and 3 months. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The page says tests or procedures unrelated to the study remain the owner's responsibility. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/radiofrequency-therapy-pain-management-dogs) The institution page does not explicitly confirm current enrollment; ask the team before planning a visit.

## What dog arthritis studies usually ask for

Osteoarthritis is one of the most common chronic, painful conditions in dogs, and veterinarians diagnose it with an orthopedic exam and X-rays, which can show joint fluid buildup, bony spurs and changes in the bone under the cartilage ([Merck Veterinary Manual, professional version](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats)). Studies want the diagnosis confirmed because they need to compare similar dogs. The Animal Medical Center study asks for X-ray confirmation ([AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)), and both Tennessee studies ask for X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis ([UT collar flyer](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf)).

Most studies also set limits on age, weight and general health. The Tennessee studies take dogs 1 to 8 years old and 15 to 40 kg ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Intra-Articular-Polymer-Beads-for-Hip-Dysplasia.pdf)), while the Animal Medical Center study takes dogs 3 and older from 10 to 100 lb ([AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)). Dogs with other health problems may be excluded: Tennessee, for example, excludes dogs with nerve disease or immune-related joint disease ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf)).

Expect a request to keep life steady. Studies ask that diet and supplements stay the same for a set time and that you avoid big changes such as boarding or a move during the study ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf); [AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)). The Guelph study asks that dogs already eat a dry kibble diet ([OVC](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/seal-oil-for-the-treatment-of-osteoarthritis/)).

Measurement is the heart of an arthritis study. Several of the studies above use a force plate or pressure mat, a walkway that records how much weight each leg carries; the Merck Veterinary Manual describes this as a way to get objective data on weight bearing ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats)). Owners also fill out questionnaires about how their dog moves at home. One widely used example is the Canine Brief Pain Inventory, an owner-completed questionnaire developed by University of Pennsylvania researchers that scores pain severity and how much pain interferes with daily activity ([Brown et al., JAVMA 2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2896492/)). Merck lists it among validated owner questionnaires for joint pain ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats)).

Some studies also ask a dog to wear an activity monitor on the collar for several weeks. Penn researchers found that such a monitor may be a valid way to measure changes in activity in dogs with osteoarthritis ([Brown et al., JAVMA 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20590496/)). None of the institution pages above mention activity monitors, so ask the study team what measurements they use.

Many studies use a placebo, an inactive version of the treatment, and keep both owner and evaluator unaware of which group a dog is in. The Tennessee collar study uses a placebo collar ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf)), the NC State study is double-blind ([NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/gi-supplement-clinical-study/)), and the Animal Medical Center study notes that a dog may get a placebo ([AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)). Your dog may not receive the product being tested.

## Current pain medicines and supplements

Many arthritis studies have rules about medicines a dog has taken recently. Examples from the studies above: Tennessee excludes dogs on pain medicines other than an NSAID or gabapentin and asks for a 4-week break from joint supplements before the start ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf)), and the Animal Medical Center study excludes dogs that had steroids in the last 30 days or a Librela injection in the last 2 months ([AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)).

Do not stop or change your dog's pain medicine to qualify for a study. Pain control matters for your dog's welfare, and NSAIDs are described as the most predictably effective treatment for osteoarthritis ([Merck](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats)). Any change, including a pause sometimes called a washout, is decided with your veterinarian and the study team, who can tell you whether it is safe for your dog and what they will use for pain in the meantime.

## What it costs to join

Every listing above shows cost coverage as not stated, but several institution pages describe study-covered exams, X-rays or lab work, and some describe a payment or gift card for completing the study ([UT](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf); [NC State](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/gi-supplement-clinical-study/); [AMC](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)). Care unrelated to the study is usually still yours to pay ([Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/radiofrequency-therapy-pain-management-dogs)). Coverage varies a great deal between studies, a point we cover in more detail in our guide to dog chemo costs and when a clinical trial can help. Ask for the cost terms in writing before you enroll.

## How to apply for a dog arthritis clinical trial

Most of the studies above start with an online form, a short questionnaire or a phone call, followed by a screening visit.

- **Talk with your veterinarian first.** Ask whether your dog's arthritis is confirmed on X-rays, which joints are involved, and whether a study makes sense alongside current care.

- **Gather records.** Have recent X-rays (or the report), the date of diagnosis, current weight, a list of every medicine, supplement and diet with doses, and any recent blood work. Studies often ask about these on the first form.

- **Read the institution's page closely.** Check age, weight, joint and medicine rules, the number of visits, and the location. Distance matters when a study has rechecks every 2 weeks.

- **Fill out the screening form or call.** Use the contact on the institution's page, not VetTrials. AMC uses an online form, NC State a short questionnaire and information call, Guelph a screening survey, Tennessee an email and phone contact on its flyers, and Cornell its hospital's general contacts.

- **Ask for the consent form in advance.** Read it with your veterinarian, especially the parts about placebo, medicine rules, costs and how to withdraw.

- **Keep your vet in the loop.** Ask whether the study needs records or a referral from your veterinarian, and share what you learn with them.

- **Expect a screening visit.** A dog that seems to fit on paper may still be ruled out after an exam, X-rays or blood work. That is normal and is not a judgment about your care.

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how many visits are there over what period?

- Could my dog receive a placebo, and is the real product offered afterward?

- What medicines and supplements are allowed, and who decides on any change?

- What happens if my dog's pain gets worse during the study?

- Which costs does the study cover, and which are mine? Is there a payment for completing it?

- What measurements will you take (X-rays, gait analysis, blood work, questionnaires, activity monitors)?

- Can my dog leave the study at any time, and what happens then?

- Will you share results with me and my veterinarian?

## What "recruiting" means here

"Recruiting" here is the label in the VetTrials database checked November 3, 2026. Some institution pages and older flyers do not give a current enrollment status. The label does not mean your dog qualifies or that a spot is open today. Studies fill, pause and close, sometimes before a page is updated. Confirm the current status and eligibility directly with the institution and with your veterinarian.

## New studies open over time

Arthritis studies come and go throughout the year, and the list above will change. You can rerun the [dog arthritis search](https://vettrials.org/?q=arthritis&species=dog&status=recruiting) whenever you like, and [check alert availability](https://vettrials.org/alerts) for notifications about new listings. If your dog is not a fit for any current study, ask your veterinarian to keep an eye out too.

## Sources

- [Osteoarthritis in Dogs and Cats, Merck Veterinary Manual, professional version](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/musculoskeletal-system/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats/osteoarthritis-in-dogs-and-cats)
- [Ability of the Canine Brief Pain Inventory to detect response to treatment in dogs with osteoarthritis, JAVMA 2008 (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2896492/)
- [Use of an activity monitor to detect response to treatment in dogs with osteoarthritis, JAVMA 2010 (PubMed)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20590496/)
- [Seeking Dogs with Arthritis for a Joint Supplement Study, Animal Medical Center](https://www.amcny.org/seeking-dogs-with-arthritis-for-a-joint-supplement-study/)
- [Seal oil osteoarthritis study, Ontario Veterinary College](https://ovcclinicaltrials.uoguelph.ca/seal-oil-for-the-treatment-of-osteoarthritis/)
- [GI Supplement Clinical Study, NC State College of Veterinary Medicine](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/gi-supplement-clinical-study/)
- [Collar for Lameness and Osteoarthritis study flyer, University of Tennessee](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Collar-for-Lameness-and-Osteoarthritis.pdf)
- [Intra-Articular Polymer Beads for Hip Dysplasia study flyer, University of Tennessee](https://vetmed.tennessee.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/UTCVM_CARES-CLINICAL-TRIAL_Intra-Articular-Polymer-Beads-for-Hip-Dysplasia.pdf)
- [Radiofrequency Therapy for Pain Management in Dogs, Cornell University](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/hospitals/clinical-trials/radiofrequency-therapy-pain-management-dogs)

body:
If you searched for a dog cancer vaccine, you probably want one of two things: the licensed melanoma vaccine your veterinarian can give, or a clinical trial testing a newer vaccine or immunotherapy. This page covers both. It explains the status of the best-known licensed, conditionally licensed and formerly licensed products in the United States, with the date and source for each status, then lists the cancer vaccine and immunotherapy studies labeled recruiting in the VetTrials trial database snapshot checked November 1, 2026.

The products and studies described here are treatments for dogs already diagnosed with cancer. The practical next step is to share this page with your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist, because most of these options depend on cancer type, stage and timing around surgery. You can also run the [live vaccine search](https://vettrials.org/?q=vaccine&species=dog&status=recruiting) for the current list.

## Dog cancer vaccine status: licensed or investigational (as of November 1, 2026)

In the United States, vaccines and other products that work through the immune system are licensed as veterinary biologics by the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) Center for Veterinary Biologics, or CVB, under the Virus-Serum-Toxin Act ([CVB Notice 17-16, USDA APHIS](https://usbiotechnologyregulation.mrp.usda.gov/sites/default/files/notice_17_16.pdf)). The FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine notes that animal biologicals are covered by both the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Virus-Serum-Toxin Act, and that the two agencies decide jurisdiction product by product ([FDA, Animal Biologicals](https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/products/animal-biologicals)). That is why the products below have USDA licenses rather than FDA approvals.

### What a USDA conditional license means

A full USDA license requires a product to be shown pure, safe, potent and effective. A conditional license is a faster route for an emergency, a limited market or another special circumstance. The product must still be pure and safe, but the efficacy bar is a "reasonable expectation of efficacy" rather than full proof ([CVB Notice 17-16](https://usbiotechnologyregulation.mrp.usda.gov/sites/default/files/notice_17_16.pdf); [9 CFR 102.6](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2008-title9-vol1/pdf/CFR-2008-title9-vol1-sec102-6.pdf)). A conditional license is issued for a set period, and USDA either reissues it or lets it end based on the company's progress toward a full license ([9 CFR 102.6](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2008-title9-vol1/pdf/CFR-2008-title9-vol1-sec102-6.pdf)). In plain words: a conditionally licensed product can be used, but the evidence behind it is still being gathered.

The CVB publishes a list of licensed veterinary biological products. The edition used below was prepared July 6, 2026, and marks conditional licenses with an asterisk ([USDA CVB, Veterinary Biological Products: Licensees and Permittees](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)). The list also includes other immune-based products that this page does not cover, so ask your veterinarian about any product not named here.

### Canine melanoma vaccine (Oncept): licensed

- **What it is:** Canine Melanoma Vaccine, DNA, sold as Oncept. The licensee named by USDA is Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health USA Inc. ([USDA APHIS summary of studies, compiled May 16, 2024](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/124-9240d0.pdf)). It is still on the CVB list prepared July 6, 2026, with no conditional marker ([USDA CVB product list](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)).
- **History:** It was conditionally licensed by the CVB in 2007 and fully licensed in 2010 ([Pellin, Veterinary Sciences, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9693055/)).
- **Who it is for:** The manufacturer describes it as an aid in extending survival times of dogs with stage II or stage III oral melanoma for which local disease control has been achieved, meaning the visible tumor has already been treated, usually with surgery ([Boehringer Ingelheim, Oncept](https://animalhealth.boehringer-ingelheim.com/pets/canine/products/therapeutics/oncept)).
- **How it is given:** In the licensing study, dogs received four doses two weeks apart after surgery, then a booster every six months, given into a rear leg muscle with the Vet Jet transdermal vaccination system ([USDA APHIS summary of studies](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/124-9240d0.pdf)). Clinics buy it through an application process with the manufacturer ([Boehringer Ingelheim, Oncept](https://animalhealth.boehringer-ingelheim.com/pets/canine/products/therapeutics/oncept)).
- **What the evidence looks like:** A 2022 literature review concluded that the vaccine is safe but that the published data fall short of definitive proof that it improves disease-free intervals or survival ([Pellin, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9693055/)). Ask an oncologist how it fits your dog's situation.

### ELIAS Cancer Immunotherapy (ECI) for osteosarcoma: USDA-licensed, check the license type

- **What it is:** A treatment that combines a vaccine made from the dog's own tumor cells with the dog's own T cells, which are collected, activated and given back ([ELIAS Animal Health](https://eliasanimalhealth.com/)).
- **Status:** ELIAS announced on March 19, 2025 that ECI received approval from the USDA CVB for the treatment of canine osteosarcoma and that it is distributed under an Autologous Prescription Product license ([ELIAS Animal Health](https://eliasanimalhealth.com/news/eci-receives-full-approval-as-treatment-for-bone-cancer-in-dogs/)). On the CVB list prepared July 6, 2026, ELIAS's Autologous Prescription Product entry carries the asterisk the list uses for conditional licenses ([USDA CVB product list](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)). ELIAS's announcement text does not itself say whether the license is full or conditional, although its web address and some press coverage describe it as full approval. Ask ELIAS or your oncologist which license currently applies.
- **Timing matters:** The decision has to be made before surgery, because tumor tissue must be collected to make the vaccine, and treatment is given at authorized treatment centers ([ELIAS Animal Health](https://eliasanimalhealth.com/news/eci-receives-full-approval-as-treatment-for-bone-cancer-in-dogs/)).

### Gilvetmab (anti-PD-1 antibody): conditional license

- **What it is:** A caninized antibody against PD-1, a "checkpoint" that can keep immune cells from attacking cancer. Merck Animal Health says it is for dogs with stage I to III mast cell tumors or stage II to III melanomas and is given by IV infusion over at least 30 minutes in the clinic ([Merck Animal Health, Gilvetmab](https://www.merck-animal-health-usa.com/products/gilvetmab/)).
- **Status:** Merck states that the license is conditional and that safety, efficacy and potency have not been fully evaluated ([Merck Animal Health](https://www.merck-animal-health-usa.com/products/gilvetmab/)). Gilvetmab appears with the conditional marker on the CVB list prepared July 6, 2026 ([USDA CVB product list](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)). It is also being tested in some of the studies listed below.

### Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector: not on the current list

- **History:** In December 2017 the CVB issued a conditional license for this vaccine to Antelope Valley Bios, Inc., based on field trials in dogs that had amputation and carboplatin chemotherapy. The license was set to expire after one year unless reissued ([CVB Notice 17-16](https://usbiotechnologyregulation.mrp.usda.gov/sites/default/files/notice_17_16.pdf)).
- **Now:** Neither the product nor that licensee appears on the CVB list prepared July 6, 2026 ([USDA CVB product list](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)). If you read about it in older articles, ask your oncologist before assuming it is available.
- **Since then:** OS Therapies says its Listeria-based vaccine, OST-HER2, was previously granted a conditional license by the CVB for canine osteosarcoma. On October 7, 2026 it announced that its animal health subsidiary had received USDA feedback ahead of a planned request for a new conditional license, and that it expects further studies would be needed for a full license ([OS Therapies press release, October 7, 2026, via Webull](https://www.webull.com/news/15708270264075264)). As of November 1, 2026 we found no announcement that a new license had been issued.

## Kinds of immunotherapy in these studies

"Immunotherapy for dogs with cancer" covers several different approaches. The terms below come up in the listings:

- **Cancer vaccines** train the immune system to recognize the cancer. Some are made from the dog's own tumor cells, such as the University of Florida mRNA study, which uses cells collected at biopsy ([University of Florida](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/mrna-vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-appendicular-osteosarcoma-currently-enrolling/)).
- **CAR-T cells** are immune cells that have had genes added so they attack cells carrying a target molecule ([University of Missouri](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)).
- **Checkpoint antibodies** such as anti-PD-1 drugs block a signal that can switch off the immune response ([Merck Animal Health](https://www.merck-animal-health-usa.com/products/gilvetmab/)).
- **Oncolytic viruses** are viruses modified to target tumors, such as the genetically modified vesicular stomatitis virus in a Minnesota lymphoma study ([University of Minnesota](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/orbit-vsv)).

Trials exist because these treatments are still being worked out in dogs. The University of Missouri notes that new anti-cancer agents in trials may not have been used in companion animals before, and the extent of possible side effects is not known ([University of Missouri](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/)). Talk with your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist about risks before enrolling.

## Cancer vaccine and immunotherapy trials listed as recruiting (checked November 1, 2026)

Each study below is listed as recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 1, 2026. That database label is not confirmation that the institution is currently enrolling. Confirm current status and eligibility with the institution and your veterinarian. VetTrials is an independent listing site, not the enrolling institution, and is not affiliated with the AVMA's registry or with the universities named here. Where the institution's own page adds detail on costs, we note it, but costs can change, so confirm them with the study team.

**Cancer vaccine studies.** These test vaccines given to dogs that already have cancer, usually alongside surgery, chemotherapy or radiation.

### [Vaccine Study for Dogs with Melanoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/148)

University of Florida, Gainesville, FL. An investigational vaccine for dogs recently diagnosed with malignant melanoma that is resectable or minimal. The university's page describes four vaccine doses about four weeks apart, plus restaging visits. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says owners pay for the vaccines, the initial exam and later visits. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/melanoma-vaccine-study-for-dogs/)

### [New vaccine for dogs with oral melanoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/188)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. Tests the safety and effectiveness of an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vaccine for oral melanoma. The university's page lists biopsy-confirmed oral malignant melanoma, age at least one year, weight at least 5 kg, and no prior melanoma vaccine (Oncept) among the criteria. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says qualifying dogs receive a $4,000 credit toward surgery or radiation at the University of Minnesota and that the study covers its other study-related visits. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/new-vaccine)

### [Vaccine Study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/145)

University of Florida, Gainesville, FL. An investigational vaccine given with standard care for dogs recently diagnosed with osteosarcoma of a limb that have not been treated yet. The university's page says dogs become eligible after their limb is amputated and sampled at UF. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says costs are the owner's responsibility, apart from up to $100 for treating injection-site reactions. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-osteosarcoma/)

### [mRNA Vaccine Study for Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/146)

University of Florida, Gainesville, FL. An RNA vaccine made from the dog's own tumor cells, given by IV with an anti-PD-1 drug. The university's page says dogs must receive radiation therapy and the tumor sample must be collected before radiation. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says the study covers vaccine-related costs while owners pay for standard diagnosis and treatment. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/mrna-vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-appendicular-osteosarcoma-currently-enrolling/)

### [Vaccine Study for Dogs with Splenic Hemangiosarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/147)

University of Florida, Gainesville, FL. An investigational vaccine given with surgery and chemotherapy for dogs recently diagnosed with splenic hemangiosarcoma. The university's page says the spleen must already be removed and staging must happen within 10 to 16 days of surgery, so timing is tight. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says costs are the owner's responsibility, apart from up to $100 for treating injection-site reactions. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://research.vetmed.ufl.edu/research-programs/clinical-trials/small-animal/oncology/vaccine-study-for-dogs-with-hemangiosarcoma/)

### [COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers](https://vettrials.org/trial/60)

University of Missouri, Columbia, MO. Evaluates an immunotherapy called the Vaccine Peptide Library in dogs with solid tumors. The listing asks for dogs weighing 15 to 60 kg with a confirmed solid tumor 2 to 8 cm across and no prior experimental therapy; mast cell tumors, cutaneous hemangiosarcomas, thyroid carcinomas and lymphomas are excluded. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)

**CAR-T and engineered T cell studies.** These collect or supply immune cells engineered to target cancer.

### [LEAH xCAR-T: Canine B-Cell Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/65)

University of Missouri, Columbia, MO. Evaluates lymphodepleting chemotherapy followed by CAR-T cells in dogs with large cell B-cell lymphoma, newly diagnosed or relapsed. The listing asks for dogs over 10 kg that are feeling well and not on immunomodulatory drugs. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)

### [CAR-T cell therapy for canines with B-cell lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/676)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. A pilot study of the safety of a CAR-T product for B-cell lymphoma. The university's page lists dogs of at least 10 kg with newly diagnosed or relapsed multicentric lymphoma, any breed except boxers. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says the study is fully funded, including the screening visit, with up to $4,000 for treating severe CAR-T side effects there and a $2,000 stipend for later cancer care at the University of Minnesota. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/car-t-cell)

### [CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/436)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO. CAR-T cell immunotherapy for dogs whose osteosarcoma has spread. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/car-t-cell-immunotherapy-for-treatment-of-metastatic-osteosarcoma-in-dogs/)

### [Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy](https://vettrials.org/trial/355)

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO. Engineered T cells combined with an oral immunotherapy. The listing names osteosarcoma and soft tissue sarcoma; the university's current page title names soft tissue sarcoma only, so ask which cancers are still being enrolled. Cost coverage noted in the listing: full. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.csuanimalcancercenter.org/clinical-trial/clinical-testing-of-canine-t-cells-engineered-to-target-osteosarcoma-and-soft-tissue-sarcoma-in-combination-with-oral-immunotherapy/)

**Checkpoint antibody, oncolytic virus and radiation combinations.**

### [ORBIT - VSV and an anti-PD-1 inhibitor for Canine Lymphoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/190)

University of Minnesota, Saint Paul, MN. Combines a genetically modified vesicular stomatitis virus with an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor for aggressive B or T cell lymphoma, either newly diagnosed or after chemotherapy was stopped because of resistance, relapse or severe side effects. The university's page lists a minimum weight of 7.5 kg, spayed or neutered dogs, and no access to livestock or horses, among other criteria. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says owners pay for the initial screening exam, bloodwork and urinalysis, and that study-related visits and treatment are covered after enrollment, up to an anticipated $10,500. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vetmed.umn.edu/departments/centers-and-programs/clinical-investigation-center/current-clinical-trials/orbit-vsv)

### [Gilvetmab for the Treatment of Primary Pulmonary Carcinoma in Dogs](https://vettrials.org/trial/64)

University of Missouri, Columbia, MO. Evaluates gilvetmab, the anti-PD-1 antibody described above, for primary lung carcinoma, in dogs with visible or microscopic disease. The listing excludes dogs with immune-mediated disease or on steroids or other immunosuppressive drugs. Cost coverage noted in the listing: partial. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://vhc.missouri.edu/small-animal-hospital/oncology/clinical-trials/current-clinical-trials/)

### [FLASH-Based Radioimmunotherapy in Canine Glioma](https://vettrials.org/trial/677)

University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA. Tests FLASH proton radiation therapy for brain tumors (gliomas), alone or with gilvetmab. The university's page says dogs must never have received gilvetmab and describes 12 follow-up visits over 11 months; it does not state an enrollment status. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says screening is the owner's cost and study procedures are covered by the sponsor once enrolled. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://www.vet.upenn.edu/clinical-trial/flash-based-radioimmunotherapy-in-canine-glioma/)

**Immune-stimulating therapies given at the tumor.**

### [Enrolling Dogs with Invasive Bladder Cancer](https://vettrials.org/trial/106)

NC State University, Raleigh, NC. An experimental immunotherapy for invasive bladder cancer (urothelial carcinoma), studied for safety and immune-stimulating effects over an eight-day study. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says staging and treatment are at no cost, but it also lists an enrollment finish date of September 30, 2026, which has passed, so confirm whether the study is still open. [Institution page](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-enrolling-dogs-with-invasive-bladder-cancer/)

### [Now Recruiting Dogs with Soft Tissue Sarcoma](https://vettrials.org/trial/95)

NC State University, Raleigh, NC. Combines surgery and standard radiation with a new immunotherapy drug called XCSgel. The study is blinded, so owners will not know whether their dog received XCSgel or a placebo. Cost coverage noted in the listing: not stated. The institution page says testing, treatment and follow-up are free for enrolled dogs. Confirm with the study team. [Institution page](https://cvm.ncsu.edu/clinical-trial/now-recruiting-dogs-with-soft-tissue-sarcoma/)

For more studies by cancer type, see our guides to canine osteosarcoma clinical trials, canine lymphoma clinical trials and dog cancer clinical trials. The cost guide covers how studies handle expenses.

## What "recruiting" means here

"Recruiting" on this page means recruiting per the VetTrials trial database, checked November 1, 2026. It does not establish the institution's current enrollment status. Studies fill, pause and close, sometimes before their pages are updated, and one study above lists an enrollment end date that has already passed. Always confirm with the study team. You can read more about how listings are gathered on the [About page](https://vettrials.org/about).

## Questions to ask the study team

- Is the study still enrolling, and how soon do you need to see my dog?
- Does my dog's cancer type, stage and treatment history fit? Does anything my dog has already had (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, Oncept, steroids, allergy drugs) rule it out?
- Does tissue need to be collected before surgery or radiation?
- Is there a placebo or control group?
- Which costs does the study cover, and which are mine, including screening, standard care and side effects?
- How many visits are needed, and how far apart?
- What side effects have been seen so far, and who handles them?
- If my dog joins, can we still use a licensed product such as Oncept or gilvetmab later, or join another study?

Bring these to your veterinarian or a board-certified veterinary oncologist as well. They can help weigh a licensed product, standard treatment and a trial for your dog.

## Sources

- [CVB Notice 17-16: Issuance of a Conditional License for Canine Osteosarcoma Vaccine, Live Listeria Vector, USDA APHIS (December 2017)](https://usbiotechnologyregulation.mrp.usda.gov/sites/default/files/notice_17_16.pdf)
- [9 CFR 102.6, Conditional licenses, Code of Federal Regulations (2008 edition), govinfo](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2008-title9-vol1/pdf/CFR-2008-title9-vol1-sec102-6.pdf)
- [Veterinary Biological Products: Licensees and Permittees, prepared July 6, 2026, USDA APHIS Center for Veterinary Biologics](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/currentprodcodebook.pdf)
- [Summary of Studies Supporting USDA Product Licensure: Canine Melanoma Vaccine, DNA, USDA APHIS (compiled May 16, 2024)](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/124-9240d0.pdf)
- [Animal Biologicals, FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine](https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/products/animal-biologicals)
- [Oncept, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health](https://animalhealth.boehringer-ingelheim.com/pets/canine/products/therapeutics/oncept)
